analysis.one_liner: Bans landlords from rejecting tenants who use federal housing vouchers and penalizes letting voucher units deteriorate.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred landlords from rejecting Section 8 voucher holders, never got a hearing or vote in any of its three House committees and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for landlords to refuse renters just because they use a federal Section 8 housing voucher, which now affects about 2.2 million low-income families. It would also fine landlords up to $100,000 for deliberately letting subsidized units fall apart to push voucher tenants out, create a HUD hotline and public complaint database, offer landlords a tax credit of up to $2,500 per low-income unit for maintenance, and fund local programs that give tenants legal help against harassment.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 2.2 million families using Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers — mostly low-income households with an average income of about $13,600, seniors, and people with disabilities — would gain the most. The bill would make it a violation of the Fair Housing Act to refuse a renter because they hold a voucher, penalize landlords who deliberately let subsidized units deteriorate to push voucher tenants out, create a HUD complaint process with public disclosure of complaints, and fund tenant anti-harassment programs offering legal help. Landlords who maintain their low-income units would gain a tax credit worth up to $2,500 per low-income unit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Section 8 voucher holders and low-income renters

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful under the Fair Housing Act to refuse to rent to someone because they hold a Section 8 housing voucher, attacking the source-of-income discrimination that leaves the voucher program with only a 60-percent success rate in placing families in housing.

Imposes a $100,000 civil penalty per violation on landlords who deliberately let a unit become indecent, unsafe, or unsanitary so it stops qualifying for federal housing assistance — a practice the bill cites amid rising property values and conversion of subsidized units to market-rate apartments — and lets affected tenants sue for $50,000 plus actual damages.

Requires HUD to staff its Multifamily Housing Complaint Line adequately, run a complaint resolution program for voucher tenants, and post each complaint publicly on a HUD website with the project identified.
Requires buildings with three or more voucher tenants to post tenant-rights notices and complaint-line numbers on every floor, with a $500-per-day penalty for failure.
Authorizes $25 million a year from 2018 through 2022 in grants to states, local governments, tribes, and nonprofits for tenant harassment prevention programs, including legal assistance.
Gives compliant landlords a tax credit of up to $2,500 per low-income unit (capped at $500,000 per taxpayer) for maintenance expenses, as an incentive to keep voucher units in good condition.

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and rental property owners would bear the cost: new federal penalties for refusing voucher holders ($100,000 per violation for deliberately degrading a unit to drive it out of federal programs), tenant lawsuits with damages starting at $50,000, posting of tenant-rights notices on every floor, and the risk of a HUD complaint file posted publicly. The tax credit for maintaining low-income units would be paid for out of federal revenue, meaning taxpayers broadly fund it. HUD would need appropriations to staff its complaint line.

drawbacks.text: The maintenance tax credit would cost the Treasury revenue and pays landlords for upkeep they are already obligated to provide under housing quality standards, and its eligibility rules turn on whether complaints were filed within 30 days, which could reward landlords in buildings where tenants are least likely to complain.

Landlords argue that accepting vouchers brings extra paperwork, inspections, and rent limits, so a federal ban on refusing voucher holders could lead some owners to withdraw from the rental market or convert units rather than participate, reducing the supply the bill is meant to protect.

The penalties are steep — $100,000 per violation and $500 per day for a missing notice — which an honest supporter would acknowledge raises the risk of disputes over what counts as an intentional act versus ordinary deferred maintenance.
The bill's notice-posting and complaint-line provisions apply only to buildings with five or more units, leaving tenants in smaller buildings without those protections.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 2.2 million families relying on Section 8 vouchers, the core protection — a federal ban on refusing tenants because they hold a voucher — addresses a well-documented barrier: the program finds housing for only about 60 percent of voucher holders. The complaint system, public disclosure, and anti-harassment grants are practical supports for tenants with little individual power. The design has real soft spots: the tax credit subsidizes landlords for maintenance they already owe their tenants, the strongest penalties could invite disputes over intent, and the bill leaves small landlords largely untouched. On balance, the benefits to low-income renters outweigh those costs, but the mechanism it died with means none of this was ever weighed on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, none of them ever acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, and referred to three committees: Financial Services, Ways and Means, and Judiciary.
None of the three committees held a hearing, marked up, or voted on the bill at any point during the two-year Congress.
The bill gathered 15 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never reached the House floor for a vote.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with no further action recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and rental property owners are better off: they never faced the proposed ban on rejecting voucher holders, the penalties for letting subsidized units deteriorate, the posted tenant-rights notices, or the public complaint database. No one gained the protections the bill would have provided voucher holders.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords who avoided new federal obligations

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill's sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsor or floor action ever appeared.

industries.note: The bill would have banned landlords from rejecting voucher holders as tenants, imposed penalties up to $100,000 for deliberately degrading units to disqualify them from federal programs, exposed them to tenant lawsuits, and posted their complaint records publicly. It would also have given landlords a new tax credit worth up to $2,500 per low-income unit for maintenance costs, and landlords who played by the rules could have gained from it — but the industry's core interest in keeping full discretion over whom to rent to ran against the tenants the bill protects.

Nonprofit affordable-housing organizations would have been eligible for federal grants to run tenant anti-harassment programs offering legal help, counseling, and complaint services, funded at up to $25 million a year.
